subject: Checking and or improving a mixture of gamma and exponential

messages.author: 0331d36387a92109
messages.subject: Checking and or improving a mixture of gamma and exponential
parts:
I have been working on implementing a mixture of a gamma and exponential in stan to describe the distribution of latency-to-first response in fixed-interval schedules of reinforcement.  Below is the code I came up with after consulting the manual, you can ignore anything related to trial at this point (trial will become important in a later version in which the mixture model has to change as a function of trial into the session).

//Theoretical Model of Latencies
//Code for Sparse Data Structure
//Current setup for only one group

data {

int<lower = 0> G; //Number of Groups = 1 at this time
int<lower = 0> S; // Number of Subjects per group
int<lower = 0> Trial; //Total Number of Trials
int<lower = 0> O_1; //Number of Total Obersations in group 1
int<lower = 0, upper =Trial> FI30trial_idx[O_1]; //Trial Array
int<lower = 1, upper = S> FI30ss[O_1]; //Subject Array
real FI30y[O_1]; //Latency Array
}

parameters {

// Individual Subject Parameters
//For Group 1
real<lower = 0> epsilon_1[S];
real<lower = 0> c_1 [S];
real<lower = 0> K_1[S];
real<lower = 0> H_1[S]; 

//Group Level Parameters
//Shape, and Means
real<lower = 0> epsilonmu[G];
real<lower = 0> cmu[G];
real<lower = 0> epsilonmu_K[G];
real<lower = 0> Hmu[G];
// Scale, Variances, SD
real<lower = 0> epsilonsigma[G];
real<lower = 0> csigma[G];
real<lower = 0> epsilonsigma_K[G];
real<lower = 0> Hsigma[G]; 


}



model {



//Prior Distributions
 epsilonmu ~ uniform(0,100);
 epsilonsigma ~ inv_gamma(.5,.5);
 cmu ~ uniform(0,100);
 csigma ~ inv_gamma(.5,.5);
 epsilonmu_K ~ uniform(0,100);
 epsilonsigma_K ~ inv_gamma(.5,.5);
 Hmu ~ uniform(0,100);
 Hsigma  ~ inv_gamma(.5,.5);


//Sampling for Individual Parameters
//In Group 1
epsilon_1 ~ lognormal(epsilonmu[1],epsilonsigma[1]);
c_1 ~ lognormal(cmu[1],csigma[1]);
K_1 ~ lognormal(epsilonmu_K[1], epsilonsigma_K[1]);
H_1 ~ lognormal(Hmu[1],Hsigma[1]); 



//Single Gamma
//for (oo1 in 1:O_1) {
//  FI30y[oo1]~ gamma(1 + epsilon_1[FI30ss[oo1]],c_1[FI30ss[oo1]]); 
//}

//Mixture of Gamma and Exponential 

for (oo1 in 1:O_1) {

increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(log((H_1[FI30ss[oo1]]/(H_1[FI30ss[oo1]] + 1))) + gamma_log(FI30y[oo1], 1 + epsilon_1[FI30ss[oo1]], c_1[FI30ss[oo1]]), 
                   log(1-(H_1[FI30ss[oo1]]/(H_1[FI30ss[oo1]] + 1))) + exponential_log(FI30y[oo1], K_1[FI30ss[oo1]]))); 

}




}


Currently, this model, over 8 subjects (each with 295 data points; I chose the sparse data structure so that this code, once finalized, can be applied to data sets in which animals do not have the same number of data points) takes roughly 1 hour to fit. Additionally, some of the posterior distributions (which are nice unimodal slightly skewed distributions) have means substantially off from those estimated via MLE.  My concern is that the duration of time it takes to run and the incongruity of the posterior distributions with MLE may be because of the priors I chose (which were informed by articles by Browne & Draper (2006), although I have yet to try the half-cauchy prior as suggested by Gelman (2006) or an inappropriate specification of the mixture model or even perhaps my parameterization of the model, e.g. weights of the two distributions are q = H/(H+1) * gamma and 1-q = 1-(H/(H+1)) * exponential or forcing the gamma shape parameter to have a minimum of 1.

Any advice would be much appreciated, and I can provide output and the csv file with data if necessary.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Checking and or improving a mixture of gamma and exponential
parts:
Did you compute the MLE with the same model in Stan?

Did the MCMC converge?

There's a problem with your model in that your parameter
declarations don't match the support in the model block:

> epsilonmu ~ uniform(0,100);

That should have an uppper=100 declaration if you insist
on this interval-constrained prior.

It helps to do the algebra on the log scale, too, so that this.

> increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(log((H_1[FI30ss[oo1]]/(H_1[FI30ss[oo1]] + 1))) + gamma_log(FI30y[oo1], 1 + epsilon_1[FI30ss[oo1]], c_1[FI30ss[oo1]]),
log(1-(H_1[FI30ss[oo1]]/(H_1[FI30ss[oo1]] + 1))) + exponential_log(FI30y[oo1], K_1[FI30ss[oo1]])));

so instead of log(a/(1 + b)), use log(a) - log1p(b).

It's much more stable.

- Bob

parts:
Hi Bob,

Thanks for the feedback. When fitting the model using MLE I did not use STAN rather I used some functions in Matlab, thus they may not be directly comparable. With that said, the fit of my mixture via the Bayes  procedure did converge (r_hat = 1) for all parameters. 

Concerning support of parameters, I am not beholden to the uniform(0,100). I chose it because I do not have any prior information about what those hyperparameters should be and just wanted relatively flat priors so that the data could drive the solution. Would there by a a more principled way to specify them to better reflect my prior beliefs so that I can avoid having to make some claim about the upper limit of the hyperparameters?

For the algebra, I added a transformed parameter block where I do the following (to limit the amount of algebra in the increment_log_prob function
transformed parameters {

real<lower = 0, upper = 1> q[O_1];
real<lower = 0> epsilon_p1[O_1];
for (oo1 in 1:O_1) {

q[oo1] <- (H_1[FI30ss[oo1]]/(H_1[FI30ss[oo1]] + 1));
    epsilon_p1[oo1] <- (epsilon_1[FI30ss[oo1]] + 1); 

  }

}

Such that the model  is now

//Mixture of Gamma and Exponential 

for (oo1 in 1:O_1) {

increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(log(q[oo1]) + gamma_log(FI30y[oo1], epsilon_p1[oo1], c_1[FI30ss[oo1]]), 
                            log(1-q[oo1]) + exponential_log(FI30y[oo1], K_1[FI30ss[oo1]])));

Will this improve stability or would it still be better to do the algebra on the log scale?

> log(1-q[oo1]) + exponential_log(FI30y[oo1], K_1[FI30ss[oo1]])));
>
> Will this improve stability or would it still be better to do the algebra on the log scale?

It's always safer to do the algebra on the log scale for both log(q)
and log(1-q). For instance, define new variables

log_q[oo1] <- log(H_1[...]) - log1p(H_1[...]);

log1m_q[oo1] <- -log1p(H_1[...]))

You need to do some algebra on the latter to see that

1 - u/(u + 1) = 1 / (u + 1)

and work from there.

But if you're not having problems with the other alternative, then I
wouldn't worry about it.

But if you do stick with your version, use log1m(u) instead of log(1 - u)
and log1p(u) in place of log(1 + u), or even swap out all of that for
our newish binary mixture function

increment_log_prob(log_mix(q[oo1], gamma_log(...), exponential_log(...)).

But that assumes q is on the linear scale, not on the log scale.

- Bob
